raw_findings.message: The handler reads the full client-supplied `Content-Length` before applying any size limit, allowing oversized requests to exhaust server memory.
The API accepts an absent `X-Api-Key` as the empty string and saves uploads under that shared identity, allowing unauthenticated callers to create and read documents owned by it.
A nonexistent document makes `STORE.get` return `None`, after which `can_read` raises `TypeError` and the handler returns 500 instead of the expected not-found response.
Purge authorization checks only whether the `X-Admin-Key` header exists, so any caller can send an arbitrary value and delete all documents.
The `next` query parameter is copied directly into the `Location` header, so an attacker can use `/go` to redirect visitors to an arbitrary site.
The unauthenticated `/docs.html` page lists every document's title and ID, exposing metadata for documents belonging to other users.
User-controlled document titles are inserted into HTML without escaping, so a title containing markup or script executes in visitors' browsers on `/docs.html`.

Share tokens come from `random.random()`, which production startup seeds with the current integer time, making tokens predictable to an attacker who can estimate startup time and token-generation order.
Documents and usage are kept only in memory and never reloaded from the files written to disk, so restarting the service makes existing documents inaccessible and resets quota accounting.
Concurrent uploads for the same API key can all pass the quota check using the same stale usage value and collectively exceed the quota.
An upload can set `meta.format` to `object` and supply a malicious pickle, causing arbitrary code execution when `pickle.loads` runs.
A caller can make the server fetch attacker-chosen URLs, including internal services or `file://` paths, and the fetched contents are saved under that caller's key.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The handler reads the entire client-supplied Content-Length before enforcing the document quota, so a caller can send a huge body and exhaust server memory.
The API key is accepted as a self-selected owner identity without validation, so unauthenticated callers can upload and share documents and evade per-key quotas by changing or omitting the header.
The `next` value can contain decoded CR/LF characters and is written directly into the Location header, allowing an attacker to inject additional response headers.
The unauthenticated documents page lists every document title and ID, exposing potentially sensitive metadata to any visitor.
The store starts with empty in-memory document and usage maps and never reloads the files on disk, so a restart makes saved documents inaccessible and resets quota accounting.

The code validates DNS results and then lets urllib resolve the hostname again when connecting, so a rebinding hostname can pass the public-address check and resolve to a private address for the fetch.
The remote response is read completely before quota enforcement, so a public URL returning a very large body can exhaust server memory.
Purge clears usage and documents without synchronizing with uploads, so a concurrent upload can finish after the clear and leave a stored document whose bytes are not charged against quota.

raw_findings.message: The upload handler trusts the caller-provided `Content-Length` and reads that many bytes without a limit, allowing large requests to exhaust server memory or tie up request threads.

Uploads accept any caller-supplied API key, including an omitted key treated as the empty string, so callers can claim known owners' identities and unauthenticated users can share access to documents uploaded without a key.
An unknown document ID makes `STORE.get` return `None`, which `can_read` then subscripts and turns into a 500 response instead of the handled 404.
Purge is authorized by the presence of `X-Admin-Key` rather than a validated secret, so any caller can add that header and delete every document.
The `/go` endpoint places the unvalidated `next` parameter in the `Location` header, allowing an attacker to redirect visitors to an arbitrary site.
Document titles are inserted into the HTML response without escaping, so uploading a title containing HTML or JavaScript causes script execution for visitors to `/docs.html`.
Share tokens use a 48-bit value from the non-cryptographic PRNG, which the application seeds with the current timestamp, allowing attackers to predict or brute-force tokens.
Token comparison exits at the first mismatching character, exposing the matching prefix length through response timing and enabling repeated guesses to recover a share token.
The store initializes its document and usage maps empty and never reloads the saved files, so restarting the service makes existing documents inaccessible and resets quota accounting.
Concurrent uploads for the same API key can both check the same stale usage value and then overwrite each other's accounting, allowing the quota to be exceeded.
The `object` format unpickles attacker-controlled upload bytes, allowing a caller to execute arbitrary code when submitting a crafted payload.
The fetch endpoint passes an unrestricted caller-supplied URL to `urlopen`, allowing requests to internal services and local resources such as `file://` paths.
The fetch handler reads the entire remote response without a size limit or timeout, so a slow or very large response can exhaust memory or occupy a server thread indefinitely.

raw_findings.message: The handler trusts arbitrary `Content-Length` values and reads the entire body into memory, allowing a caller to exhaust server memory with a sufficiently large request.
The handler accepts any supplied API-key string, including an empty one, as an identity, so callers can create or impersonate that identity and access its documents.
The purge operation checks only whether `X-Admin-Key` is present and never validates its value, so any caller can send an arbitrary header value and delete all documents.
The `/go` endpoint puts the unvalidated `next` parameter in the `Location` header, allowing an attacker to redirect users to a malicious site.
An uploaded title is interpolated into the public HTML without escaping, so a malicious title executes script when someone visits `/docs.html`.
Share tokens come from the non-cryptographic `random` generator, which the server seeds with the startup time, making bearer tokens predictable to an attacker who can estimate that time.
The store initializes its document and usage maps empty and never reloads the files it writes, so a process restart makes existing documents and quota state unavailable.
Concurrent uploads for one API key can both read the same usage before either updates it, allowing their combined payloads to exceed the quota.
Each successful upload leaves its staged `.part` file in `tmp_dir` after copying it to the final path, allowing repeated uploads to consume unbounded disk space.
An uploader can set `meta.format` to `object` and submit a malicious pickle, causing arbitrary code execution in the server when `pickle.loads` runs.
`fetch_remote` passes the caller-controlled URL directly to `urlopen`, allowing requests to internal services and, where supported, `file://` URLs that expose local files through the saved document.
The fetch endpoint reads the entire remote response into memory before applying the quota check, so a caller can cause memory exhaustion by fetching a large response.
